title: T-SQL Exercises
description: Read each example in its lesson first. Predict the result, then check your answer. The notes explain the idea and one common mistake.

exercises.question: SELECT asks for a result. AS gives its column a name. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: SELECT returns the string as a one-cell result. AS names that result column. Text literals use single quotes.

exercises.question: DECLARE makes a local variable. T-SQL variable names start with @. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: DECLARE creates @pencils as int 3. The SELECT expression adds 2. The variable exists only in its batch or procedure scope.

exercises.question: CONCAT joins values as text. It can also convert simple number inputs to text. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: CONCAT joins the three text values without adding extra characters. Do not assume + behaves the same way with NULL and mixed types.

exercises.code:
DECLARE @score int = 8;
SELECT CASE WHEN @score >= 5 THEN 'Pass' ELSE 'Try again' END AS message;
exercises.question: CASE returns a value from the first matching branch. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The first CASE condition is true for 8. It returns Pass. CASE ends with END; it is an expression, not an IF block.

exercises.question: IF controls which SQL statements run. BEGIN and END group statements. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The IF test succeeds, so the first PRINT runs. Use BEGIN and END when a branch has several statements.

exercises.code: SELECT n FROM (VALUES (3), (1), (2)) AS numbers(n) ORDER BY n;
exercises.question: VALUES can create rows for a query. An alias names the tiny table and its column. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: VALUES creates rows 3, 1 and 2. ORDER BY sorts them into 1, 2 and 3. Use ORDER BY when the row order matters.

exercises.code: SELECT n FROM (VALUES (4), (8), (9)) AS scores(n) WHERE n >= 7 ORDER BY n;
exercises.question: WHERE keeps rows that pass a condition. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: WHERE removes 4 because it is below 7. ORDER BY keeps the remaining result in order. WHERE filters rows before they are grouped.

exercises.code: SELECT SUM(n) AS total FROM (VALUES (2), (3), (4)) AS numbers(n);
exercises.question: SUM adds a column over the selected rows. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: SUM adds the three selected numbers to make 9. SUM ignores NULL inputs; it does not treat them as a known zero.

exercises.code:
DECLARE @name varchar(20) = NULL;
SELECT COALESCE(@name, 'Guest') AS name;
exercises.question: COALESCE returns the first input that is not NULL. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The first value is NULL, so COALESCE picks Guest. Use IS NULL for a null test, not = NULL.

exercises.question: TRY_CONVERT returns NULL when this text cannot be converted to int. COALESCE then supplies zero. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: TRY_CONVERT cannot read cat as an int. Its NULL result is replaced by zero. A failed conversion is not automatically a real score of zero; choose a suitable fallback for your app.

exercises.question: WHILE repeats its block while a rule stays true. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: PRINT runs for 1, 2 and 3. SET advances the counter to stop the loop. Change the loop value so the loop eventually stops.

exercises.question: JSON_VALUE reads one simple value from JSON text using a path. What result does this example give after the setup steps?
exercises.explanation: The path $.title selects the scalar title field from the JSON object. Use valid JSON with double-quoted field names.
